opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think from the outside it looks like disorder, and sometimes from the inside too. But when I look back, I don't think I was ever following a master plan. I was following curiosity, and curiosity doesn't move in straight lines.

If you look at my path, there are a lot of turns that might not make sense on paper: going into industry research, then coming back to academia, moving between architecture design, representation learning, generative models, and now thinking more about multimodal systems and how models understand the world. People sometimes ask, "Why did you switch topics?" Or, "Why didn't you keep going in the direction that was already working?" And I think the real answer is that once something starts to feel *too* clear, once I can roughly see where it ends, I lose some of the excitement. I'm drawn to the places where things are still messy and nobody quite knows what the right question is yet.

So I've come to accept that a certain amount of disorder is the cost of doing research the way I want to do it. Research isn't like climbing a ladder. It's more like wandering through a forest. You think you're heading somewhere, then you find something more interesting off the path. If you're too disciplined about staying on the original route, you might miss the thing that actually matters.

That said, I don't think it's *pure* randomness. There's an underlying thread, at least the way I see it. Almost everything I've done comes back to one question: how do we get machines to learn good representations of the world, so that they can see, understand, and eventually reason? Architecture, self-supervised learning, diffusion, multimodal models: they're different windows into the same question. So the surface looks chaotic, but the core has been fairly stable.

And I also think, especially in this field, the environment changes so fast that rigid planning is almost a disadvantage. Five years ago, very few people would have predicted where we are now. If you lock yourself into a ten-year plan, you're betting that the world stays still, and it never does. So in some sense, being a bit disordered, being willing to change, is a way of staying honest with reality.

Of course, there's a personal side too. I'm not someone who naturally optimizes for the safest choice. Sometimes I make decisions more by feeling: this group of people is exciting, this problem keeps me up at night, this environment lets me be more free. Later I try to rationalize it. *(laughs)* But I've learned to trust that feeling a bit more over time, because the times I went against it, I usually regretted it more than the times I followed it and things got messy.

So my understanding of the disorder is: it's not something I try to eliminate. It's something I try to live with, and hopefully turn into a kind of openness. As long as the core question is still there and I still care about it, I'm okay with the path looking a little chaotic.

r001.rationale: The response describes willingly changing direction and treating some disorder as an openness to pursue curiosity, presenting it as accepted and chosen.

r002.rationale: It says rigid planning is disadvantageous because the field changes quickly, but does not attribute the disorder to the frequent impossibility of truly optimizing an outcome.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "disorder" is actually a pretty accurate word, and I've made peace with it. If you look at my path from the outside, it doesn't look like a plan. I studied at Shanghai Jiao Tong, went to UC San Diego for my PhD, then FAIR at Meta, then I left industry to go back to academia at NYU. People ask me, why would you leave a big lab with all that compute to become a professor? It sounds irrational.

But I've never really made decisions by optimizing some long-term objective. I'm a researcher, I like gradient descent, but I don't apply it to my life. Most of my choices came from a very local signal: is this problem making me curious right now, and are the people around me the kind of people I want to think with? When those two things are true, I stay. When they stop being true, I move. From the outside that looks like noise. From the inside it feels quite consistent.

There's also something about research itself. The best work I've been part of, ResNeXt, ConvNeXt, the self-supervised stuff, the diffusion transformer work, none of it came from a roadmap. It came from being a little bit annoyed by a consensus that everyone accepted too quickly. When everyone said transformers had made convolution obsolete, I wanted to check. When everyone said U-Nets were the only way to do diffusion, I wanted to check. That instinct, to go stand where the crowd isn't standing, is probably the same instinct that makes my career look disorderly.

So I'd put it this way: I try to keep my values ordered and let my trajectory stay disordered. If you fix the destination too early, you basically guarantee you'll end up somewhere everyone else already is. I'd rather preserve some entropy. Honestly, in this field, with how fast things change, I think the people who planned the most carefully five years ago are often the ones who feel most lost today.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says he lets his trajectory stay disordered and would rather preserve some entropy, presenting that disorder as a deliberate choice.

r002.rationale: The candidate says he does not optimize a long-term objective, but does not attribute his disorder to optimization being impossible.

astra-6.text:
I think the disorder comes from not having a complete picture of what I want in advance. Something interests me, I follow it, and through that experience I discover a different question. So each choice changes the way I make the next choice. It’s difficult to turn that into a neat plan.

Looking back, you can usually find a thread, but I’m a little suspicious of how tidy those explanations become. At the time, there’s uncertainty, curiosity, and chance. For me, the useful question is whether I’m choosing something because I really want to understand it, or because it seems like the choice I’m supposed to make. I can accept some disorder if I’m being honest about that.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes disorder emerging from curiosity, uncertainty, and changing interests. Saying they can accept some disorder does not present it as deliberately chosen.

r002.rationale: The candidate attributes disorder to not having a complete picture in advance and to choices changing over time. It does not say that outcomes cannot truly be optimized.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the disorder comes partly from the fact that you’re making choices before you really understand what you’re looking for. You have some curiosity, some intuition, but you don’t have a complete map. So from the outside, the path can look quite random.

But I don’t think that means the choices have no connection. Often the connection becomes clear only afterward. You try something, discover what interests you, and that changes the next question you want to pursue. There’s a kind of continuity in that, even if there isn’t a fixed plan.

For me, the important distinction is between allowing uncertainty and choosing without thinking. You can be serious about a decision without knowing where it will lead. I’m comfortable leaving some room for that.

r001.rationale: The response says Xie is comfortable leaving room for uncertainty, but does not clearly say he deliberately chose the disorder in his choices.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute the disorder to the impossibility of truly optimizing outcomes.
